bookInfo.name: New History of the Five Dynasties

title.zh: 卷三十七 伶官傳第二十五: 周匝 敬新磨 景進 史彥瓊 郭從謙
title.raw: 卷三十七 伶官傳第二十五: 周匝 敬新磨 景進 史彥瓊 郭從謙 Volume 37 Biographies 17:

sentences.zh: 嗚呼，盛衰之理，雖曰天命，豈非人事哉！

translations.literal: Alas! The principle of rise and decline—though called Heaven’s mandate—is it not rather human affairs!
translations.idiomatic: Alas! Rise and fall may be called fate—but is it not, in the end, the work of men?

sentences.zh: 原莊宗之所以得天下，與其所以失之者，可以知之矣。

translations.literal: Tracing why Zhuangzong gained the realm and why he lost it, one may know this.
translations.idiomatic: Consider how Zhuangzong won the realm and how he lost it—the answer lies there.

sentences.zh: 世言晉王之將終也，以三矢賜莊宗而告之曰：「梁，吾仇也，燕王吾所立，契丹與吾約為兄弟，而皆背晉以歸梁。

translations.literal: The world says when the Prince of Jin was near death he gave Zhuangzong three arrows and told him: “Liang is my enemy; the Prince of Yan I myself established; the Khitan and I swore brotherhood—all yet betrayed Jin to join Liang.
translations.idiomatic: Men say that as the Prince of Jin lay dying he gave Zhuangzong three arrows and said: “Liang is my foe; the Prince of Yan I raised up; the Khitan and I were sworn brothers—yet all turned from Jin to Liang.

sentences.zh: 此三者，吾遺恨也。

translations.literal: These three are my remaining hatreds.”
translations.idiomatic: These three are the debts I leave unpaid.”

sentences.zh: 與爾三矢，爾其無忘乃父之志！

translations.literal: I give you three arrows—you must not forget your father’s will!”
translations.idiomatic: Take these three arrows—do not forget your father’s charge!”

sentences.zh: 」莊宗受而藏之於廟。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong received them and stored them in the temple.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong took them and laid them in the ancestral temple.

sentences.zh: 其后用兵，則遣從事以一少牢告廟，請其矢，盛以錦囊，負而前驅，及凱旋而納之。

translations.literal: Thereafter when he took the field he sent an attendant with a young ox to report at the temple, took out the arrows, placed them in brocade bags, carried them on his back riding ahead; when he returned in triumph he put them back.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever he marched to war he sent a clerk with a young ox to announce it at the temple, drew out the arrows, packed them in brocade pouches, bore them on his back at the van—and when victory came home, returned them to their place.

sentences.zh: 方其係燕父子以組，函梁君臣之首，入于太廟，還矢先王而告以成功，其意氣之盛，可謂壯哉！

translations.literal: When he bound the Yan father and son with rope, boxed the heads of Liang’s lord and ministers, entered the Grand Temple, returned the arrows to the former king and reported success—his spirit at its height, one might say how magnificent!
translations.idiomatic: When he had bound the Yan princes with cord, cased the heads of Liang’s court, entered the Grand Temple, and given back the arrows to his father’s shade with news of triumph—what pride, what splendor!

sentences.zh: 及仇雠已滅，天下已定，一夫夜呼，亂者四應，蒼皇東出，未及見賊而士卒離散，君臣相顧，不知所歸，至於誓天断髮，泣下沾襟，何其衰也！

translations.literal: When his foes were destroyed and the realm settled, one man cried out at night and rebels answered on four sides; he fled east in panic, before he saw the enemy his soldiers scattered; lord and ministers looked at each other not knowing where to go, until they swore to Heaven and cut their hair, tears soaking their collars—how fallen!
translations.idiomatic: When his enemies were gone and the realm secure, a single shout in the night brought mutiny on every side; he fled east in disarray, his army melting away before he met the foe; court and emperor stared at one another with nowhere to turn, swearing to Heaven and shearing their hair, weeping until their robes were wet—how far he had fallen!

sentences.zh: 豈得之難而失之易歟？

translations.literal: Is gaining hard and losing easy?
translations.idiomatic: Is it hard to win the world and easy to lose it?

sentences.zh: 抑本其成敗之迹而皆自於人歟？

translations.literal: Or tracing the traces of success and failure, are they all from men?
translations.idiomatic: Or do success and ruin always trace back to human choices?

sentences.zh: 《書》曰：「滿招損，謙得益。

translations.literal: The Book says: “Fullness invites loss; modesty brings gain.”
translations.idiomatic: The Book says: “Pride invites ruin; humility brings gain.”

sentences.zh: 」憂勞可以興國，逸豫可以亡身，自然之理也。

translations.literal: Anxiety and toil can raise a state; ease and pleasure can destroy oneself—nature’s principle.
translations.idiomatic: Care and hardship can revive a kingdom; idleness and indulgence can destroy a man—that is the way of things.

sentences.zh: 故方其盛也，舉天下之豪傑莫能與之爭；

translations.literal: Thus at his height, all the heroes under Heaven could not contend with him;
translations.idiomatic: At his zenith no champion under Heaven could stand against him;

sentences.zh: 及其衰也，數十伶人困之，而身死國滅，為天下笑。

translations.literal: at his decline, a few dozen actors beset him, and he died, the state perished, and the realm laughed.
translations.idiomatic: at his fall a handful of actors brought him down—he died, his house ended, and the world mocked him.

sentences.zh: 夫禍患常積於忽微，而智勇多困於所溺，豈獨伶人也哉！

translations.literal: Calamity often gathers from the slight and minute; wisdom and courage often founder in what one drowns in—is it only actors!
translations.idiomatic: Disaster grows from tiny neglects; wit and valor drown in obsession—is that true only of actors?

sentences.zh: 作《伶官傳》。

translations.literal: [The author] composed “The Biography of Court Entertainers.”
translations.idiomatic: Hence this “Biography of Court Entertainers.”

sentences.zh: 莊宗既好俳優，又知音，能度曲，至今汾、晉之俗，往往能歌其聲，謂之「御製」者皆是也。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong both loved actors and understood music, could compose tunes—to this day the customs of Fen and Jin often sing his melodies; what is called “imperially composed” is all his.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong loved actors, knew music, and wrote songs himself—even now in Fen and Jin people still sing his tunes; whatever is called “imperial composition” is his.

sentences.zh: 其小字亞子，當時人或謂之亞次。

translations.literal: His childhood name was Yazi; men of the time sometimes called him Yaci.
translations.idiomatic: His pet name was Yazi; some called him Yaci.

sentences.zh: 又别為優名以自目，曰李天下。

translations.literal: He also took a separate actor’s name for himself, calling himself Li Tianxia—“Li Who Rules All Under Heaven.”
translations.idiomatic: He gave himself another stage name: Li Tianxia—“Li Who Owns the World.”

sentences.zh: 自其為王，至於為天子，常身與俳優杂戲於庭，伶人由此用事，遂至於亡。

translations.literal: From when he became king until he became Son of Heaven he often mixed with actors in buffoonery in the courtyard; actors thereby wielded power, until ruin.
translations.idiomatic: From prince to emperor he played the fool with actors in the palace yard; through them power passed into their hands—and on to destruction.

sentences.zh: 皇后劉氏素微，其父劉叟，賣藥善卜，號劉山人。

translations.literal: Empress Liu was of humble birth; her father, Old Liu, sold medicine and was skilled at divination, and was called Liu the Mountain Man.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Liu came from nothing; her father Old Liu sold herbs and told fortunes, known as Liu the Mountain Man.

sentences.zh: 劉氏性悍，方與諸姬爭寵，常自恥其世家，而特諱其事。

translations.literal: Liu was fierce in nature; contending with the concubines for favor, she was often ashamed of her family and especially concealed the matter.
translations.idiomatic: The empress was proud and jealous, fighting the palace women for favor; she hated her low origins and hid them at all costs.

sentences.zh: 莊宗乃為劉叟衣服，自負蓍囊藥篋，使其子繼岌提破帽而隨之，造其卧内，曰：「劉山人来省女。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong dressed as Old Liu, carried a divination bag and medicine box on his back, had his son Jiji wear a battered hat and follow, went to her bedchamber and said, “Liu the Mountain Man has come to visit his daughter.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong put on Old Liu’s clothes, shouldered the diviner’s pouch and medicine chest, sent his son Jiji after him in a torn cap, and walked into her chamber: “Liu the Mountain Man is here to see his girl.”

sentences.zh: 」劉氏大怒，笞繼岌而逐之。

translations.literal: Liu flew into a rage, flogged Jiji, and drove them out.
translations.idiomatic: The empress erupted, beat Jiji, and threw them out.

sentences.zh: 宫中以為笑樂。

translations.literal: The palace took it as a great jest.
translations.idiomatic: The inner court roared with laughter.

sentences.zh: 其戰於胡柳也，嬖伶周匝為梁人所得。

translations.literal: At the battle of Huliu his favorite actor Zhou Za was captured by Liang.
translations.idiomatic: At Huliu his beloved actor Zhou Za fell into Liang’s hands.

sentences.zh: 其後滅梁入汴，周匝謁於馬前，莊宗得之喜甚，賜以金帛，勞其良苦。

translations.literal: Later, having destroyed Liang and entered Bian, Zhou Za paid respects before his horse; Zhuangzong was overjoyed to have him back, bestowed gold and silks, and consoled his bitter hardship.
translations.idiomatic: When Liang fell and he entered Bian, Zhou Za knelt before his horse; Zhuangzong was delighted, heaped gifts on him, and praised his endurance.

sentences.zh: 周匝對曰：「身陷仇人，而得不死以生者，教坊使陳俊、内園栽接使儲德源之力也。

translations.literal: Zhou Za replied: “Trapped among enemies yet living—I owe my life to Director of the Music Bureau Chen Jun and Inner Garden Grafting Commissioner Chu Deyuan.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhou Za said: “I was in the enemy’s grip and should have died—Chen Jun of the Music Bureau and Chu Deyuan of the Inner Garden saved me.”

sentences.zh: 願乞二州以報此兩人。

translations.literal: I beg two prefectures to repay these two men.”
translations.idiomatic: Grant me two prefectures for these two men.”

sentences.zh: 」莊宗皆許以為刺史。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong promised them both as regional governors.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong agreed to make each of them a prefect.

sentences.zh: 郭崇韜諫曰：「陛下所與共取天下者，皆英豪忠勇之士。

translations.literal: Guo Chongtao remonstrated: “Those with whom Your Majesty took the realm are all heroic, loyal, brave men.
translations.idiomatic: Guo Chongtao objected: “The men who won the realm with you are heroes—loyal and fierce.

sentences.zh: 今大功始就，封賞未及於一人，而先以伶人為刺史，恐失天下心。

translations.literal: Great merit has just been achieved; rewards have not yet reached a single man, yet you would first make actors regional governors—I fear losing the hearts of the realm.”
translations.idiomatic: The war is barely won and not one soldier has been rewarded, yet actors are to become prefects—you will lose the army’s heart.”

sentences.zh: 不可！

translations.literal: It cannot be done!”
translations.idiomatic: You must not do this!”

sentences.zh: 」因格其命。

translations.literal: Thus he blocked the orders.
translations.idiomatic: He held the edicts back.

sentences.zh: 踰年，而伶人屢以為言，莊宗謂崇韜曰：「吾已許周匝矣，使吾慙見此二人。

translations.literal: A year passed; the actors raised the matter again and again. Zhuangzong told Guo Chongtao: “I already promised Zhou Za—I would be ashamed to face these two men.
translations.idiomatic: A year later the actors pressed him again. Zhuangzong said to Guo Chongtao: “I gave Zhou Za my word—I cannot bear to meet those two men now.

sentences.zh: 公言雖正，然當為我屈意行之。

translations.literal: Your words are correct, yet you must bend your intent and carry this out for me.”
translations.idiomatic: You are right—but for my sake, swallow your objections and do it.”

sentences.zh: 」卒以俊為景州刺史、德源為憲州刺史。

translations.literal: In the end Jun was made prefect of Jingzhou and Deyuan prefect of Xianzhou.
translations.idiomatic: At last Chen Jun became prefect of Jingzhou and Chu Deyuan prefect of Xianzhou.

sentences.zh: 莊宗好畋獵，獵于中牟，踐民田。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong loved hunting; hunting at Zhongmou he trampled the people’s fields.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong loved the chase; at Zhongmou he rode through the farmers’ crops.

sentences.zh: 中牟縣令當馬切諫，為民請，莊宗怒，叱縣令去，將殺之。

translations.literal: The Zhongmou magistrate blocked his horse and urged him strongly, pleading for the people; Zhuangzong grew angry, shouted at the magistrate to leave, and was about to kill him.
translations.idiomatic: The county magistrate seized his bridle and pleaded for his people; Zhuangzong raged, ordered him away, and prepared to execute him.

sentences.zh: 伶人敬新磨知其不可，乃率諸伶走追縣令，擒至馬前責之曰：「汝為縣令，獨不知吾天子好獵邪？

translations.literal: The actor Jing Xinmo knew this could not stand; he led the other actors running after the magistrate, seized him before the horse, and rebuked him: “You are a magistrate—do you alone not know our Son of Heaven loves hunting?
translations.idiomatic: Jing Xinmo saw the danger and rallied the actors to chase the magistrate down, drag him before the horse, and scold him: “You hold office under Heaven’s Son—do you not know he loves to hunt?

sentences.zh: 奈何縱民稼穑以供税賦！

translations.literal: Why let the people plant grain to supply taxes and levies!
translations.idiomatic: Why let peasants sow grain for taxes!

sentences.zh: 何不饑汝縣民而空此地，以備吾天子之馳騁？

translations.literal: Why not starve the people of your county and empty this land to ready it for our Son of Heaven’s riding!
translations.idiomatic: Why not starve your whole county and clear the ground for the emperor’s horses!

sentences.zh: 汝罪當死！

translations.literal: Your crime deserves death!”
translations.idiomatic: You deserve to die!”

sentences.zh: 」因前請亟行刑，諸伶共唱和之。

translations.literal: He stepped forward asking for immediate execution; the other actors all chimed in.
translations.idiomatic: He pressed for instant punishment; the rest of the actors joined the chorus.

sentences.zh: 莊宗大笑，縣令乃得免去。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong laughed loudly; the magistrate thereby escaped punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong burst out laughing—and the magistrate was spared.

sentences.zh: 莊宗嘗與羣優戲于庭，四顧而呼曰：「李天下，李天下何在？

translations.literal: Zhuangzong once played with the actors in the courtyard, looked about, and called: “Li Tianxia—where is Li Tianxia?”
translations.idiomatic: Once, playing with the actors in the yard, Zhuangzong glanced around and shouted: “Li Tianxia! Where is Li Tianxia?”

sentences.zh: 」新磨遽前以手批其頰。

translations.literal: Xinmo swiftly stepped forward and slapped his cheek.
translations.idiomatic: Xinmo darted up and struck him across the face.

sentences.zh: 莊宗失色，左右皆恐，羣伶亦大驚駭，共持新磨詰曰：「汝奈何批天子頰？

translations.literal: Zhuangzong changed color; his attendants were all afraid; the actors were greatly alarmed and together seized Xinmo, demanding: “How dare you slap the Son of Heaven’s cheek?”
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong went pale; his attendants froze in terror; the actors cried out and seized Xinmo: “How dare you strike the emperor’s face?”

sentences.zh: 」新磨對曰：「李天下者，一人而已，復誰呼邪！

translations.literal: Xinmo replied: “Li Who Rules All Under Heaven is but one person—who else are you calling?”
translations.idiomatic: Xinmo answered: “There is only one Li Who Owns the World—who else did you mean?”

sentences.zh: 」於是左右皆笑，莊宗大喜，賜與新磨甚厚。

translations.literal: Then the attendants all laughed; Zhuangzong was greatly pleased and richly rewarded Xinmo.
translations.idiomatic: The court burst into laughter; Zhuangzong was delighted and heaped gifts on Xinmo.

sentences.zh: 新磨嘗奏事殿中，殿中多惡犬，新磨去，一犬起逐之，新磨倚柱而呼曰：「陛下毋縱兒女嚙人！

translations.literal: Xinmo once reported matters in the hall; there were many fierce dogs in the hall. As Xinmo left, one dog rose and chased him; Xinmo leaned on a pillar and called: “Your Majesty, do not let your sons and daughters bite people!”
translations.idiomatic: Reporting to the throne one day, Xinmo was set upon by the palace dogs. He clung to a pillar and yelled: “Your Majesty—control your children! They bite!”

sentences.zh: 」莊宗家世夷狄，夷狄之人諱狗，故新磨以此譏之。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong’s family was of barbarian descent; barbarians taboo dogs, so Xinmo used this to mock him.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong’s line was Turkic; Turkic peoples shun talk of dogs—so Xinmo was needling his origin.

sentences.zh: 莊宗大怒，彎弓注矢將射之，新磨急呼曰：「陛下無殺臣！

translations.literal: Zhuangzong was greatly angry, bent his bow, aimed an arrow, and was about to shoot; Xinmo cried urgently: “Your Majesty must not kill me!
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong snatched up his bow to shoot him; Xinmo screamed: “Do not kill me, Majesty!

sentences.zh: 臣與陛下為一体，殺之不祥！

translations.literal: I and Your Majesty are one body—to kill me is ill-omened!”
translations.idiomatic: You and I are one—slay me and you slay yourself!”

sentences.zh: 」莊宗大驚，問其故，對曰：「陛下开國，改元同光，天下皆謂陛下同光帝。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong was greatly startled and asked the reason; he replied: “Your Majesty founded the state and changed the era to Tongguang; all under Heaven call Your Majesty Emperor Tongguang.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong stared, baffled; Xinmo said: “You founded the dynasty and named the era Tongguang—‘Shared Radiance’—so the world calls you the Emperor of Shared Radiance.

sentences.zh: 且同，銅也，若殺敬新磨，則同無光矣。

translations.literal: Moreover tong means copper—if you kill Jing Xinmo, then ‘tong’ has no ‘guang’!”
translations.idiomatic: Tong also means bronze—kill Jing Xinmo and you snuff out the guang in Tongguang!”

sentences.zh: 」莊宗大笑，乃释之。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong laughed loudly and released him.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong roared with laughter and let him go.

sentences.zh: 然時諸伶，獨新磨尤善俳，其語最著，而不聞其佗過惡。

translations.literal: Yet among the actors of the time only Xinmo was especially skilled at buffoonery; his wit was most renowned, and one heard no other faults from him.
translations.idiomatic: Of all the actors, only Xinmo was a true master of the jest—his lines are still remembered, and no other scandal attaches to his name.

sentences.zh: 其敗政亂國者，有景進、史彦瓊、郭門高三人為最。

translations.literal: Those who ruined government and threw the state into chaos were foremost Jing Jin, Shi Yanqiong, and Men Gao—three men.
translations.idiomatic: The men who wrecked the realm were three: Jing Jin, Shi Yanqiong, and Men Gao.

sentences.zh: 是時，諸伶人出入宫掖，侮弄縉紳，羣臣憤嫉，莫敢出氣，或反相附託，以希恩倖，四方藩鎮，貨賂交行，而景進最居中用事。

translations.literal: At that time actors came and went in the inner palace, insulted and toyed with the gentry; ministers burned with resentment yet dared not breathe; some instead attached themselves seeking favor; regional commanders everywhere exchanged bribes—and Jing Jin held the most power at court.
translations.idiomatic: Actors wandered the inner quarters, mocking officials; the court seethed but no one spoke; some ministers flattered them for favor; governors bought their goodwill with gifts—and Jing Jin ruled from the center.

sentences.zh: 莊宗遣進等出訪民間，事無大小皆以聞。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong sent Jin and others to investigate among the people; matters large and small were all reported.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong sent Jin and his crew to spy on the realm; nothing was too small to reach his ear.

sentences.zh: 每進奏事殿中，左右皆屏退，軍機國政皆與參決，三司使孔謙兄事之，呼為「八哥」。

translations.literal: Whenever Jin reported in the hall the attendants withdrew; military secrets and state affairs were all decided with him; Kong Qian, director of the Three Offices, treated him as an elder brother and called him “Eighth Elder Brother.”
translations.idiomatic: When Jin came to report, the room was cleared; he sat in on war and policy; Kong Qian of the Three Offices called him “Eighth Brother” and bowed to him like kin.

sentences.zh: 莊宗初入洛，居唐故宫室，而嬪御未備。

translations.literal: When Zhuangzong first entered Luoyang he dwelt in Tang’s old palace, but his consorts were not yet sufficient.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong entered Luoyang and moved into the old Tang palaces, but his harem was still thin.

sentences.zh: 閹宦希旨，多言宫中夜見鬼物，相驚恐，莊宗問所以禳之者，因曰：「故唐時，後宫萬人，今空宫多怪，當實以人乃息。

translations.literal: Eunuchs currying favor said that at night ghosts were seen in the palace and all were afraid; Zhuangzong asked how to exorcise them. They said: “In old Tang the rear palace held ten thousand; now the empty halls breed spirits—fill them with living people and the hauntings will cease.”
translations.idiomatic: Eunuchs told him the palace was haunted at night; he asked how to cleanse it. They said: “Tang’s inner court held ten thousand women—emptiness breeds ghosts. Put real people in the halls and the shadows will go.”

sentences.zh: 」莊宗欣然。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong was pleased.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong liked the plan.

sentences.zh: 其後幸鄴，乃遣進等採鄴美女千人，以充後宫。

translations.literal: Later, on an excursion to Ye, he sent Jin and others to gather a thousand beauties of Ye to fill the rear palace.
translations.idiomatic: On a later visit to Ye he sent Jin and the rest to collect a thousand Ye beauties for the harem.

sentences.zh: 而進等緣以為姦，軍士妻女因而逃逸者數千人。

translations.literal: But Jin and the others used the mission for debauchery; soldiers’ wives and daughters fled by the thousands.
translations.idiomatic: Jin and his men turned the roundup into rape; thousands of soldiers’ wives and daughters ran.

sentences.zh: 莊宗還洛，進载鄴女千人以從，道路相屬，男女無别。

translations.literal: When Zhuangzong returned to Luoyang, Jin loaded a thousand Ye women to follow; the road was unbroken, men and women undistinguished.
translations.idiomatic: Returning to Luoyang, Jin marched a thousand Ye women in his train; the roads were choked, sex and order forgotten.

sentences.zh: 魏王繼岌已破蜀，劉皇后聽宦者讒言，遣繼岌賊殺郭崇韜。

translations.literal: Prince of Wei Jiji had already conquered Shu; Empress Liu, listening to eunuch slander, sent Jiji to assassinate Guo Chongtao.
translations.idiomatic: Prince of Wei Jiji had taken Shu; the empress, swayed by eunuchs, ordered Jiji to murder Guo Chongtao.

sentences.zh: 崇韜素嫉伶人，常裁抑之，伶人由此皆樂其死。

translations.literal: Chongtao had always resented the actors and often restrained them; the actors therefore all rejoiced at his death.
translations.idiomatic: Chongtao had long hated the actors and curbed them—the actors celebrated when he died.

sentences.zh: 皇弟存乂，崇韜之壻也，進讒於莊宗曰：「存乂且反，為婦翁報仇。

translations.literal: The imperial younger brother Cunyi was Chongtao’s son-in-law; Jin slandered him to Zhuangzong: “Cunyi is about to rebel, to avenge his father-in-law.”
translations.idiomatic: Imperial brother Cunyi was Chongtao’s son-in-law; Jin whispered to Zhuangzong: “Cunyi will rise to avenge his wife’s father.”

sentences.zh: 」乃囚而殺之。

translations.literal: He was imprisoned and killed.
translations.idiomatic: They seized him and put him to death.

sentences.zh: 朱友謙，以梁河中降晉者，及莊宗入洛，伶人皆求賂於友謙，友謙不能給而辭焉。

translations.literal: Zhu Youqian had surrendered Hezhong of Liang to Jin; when Zhuangzong entered Luoyang the actors all sought bribes from Youqian; Youqian could not pay and declined.
translations.idiomatic: Zhu Youqian, who had brought Hezhong over from Liang, was shaken down by every actor when Zhuangzong reached Luoyang; he could not pay and refused.

sentences.zh: 進乃讒友謙曰：「崇韜且誅，友謙不自安，必反，宜幷誅之。

translations.literal: Jin then slandered Youqian: “Chongtao is about to be executed; Youqian is ill at ease and will surely rebel—he should be executed together.”
translations.idiomatic: Jin accused him: “With Chongtao gone, Youqian is uneasy—he will rebel. Kill him too.”

sentences.zh: 」於是及其將五六人皆族滅之，天下不勝其冤。

translations.literal: Thus Youqian and his generals, five or six men, were all exterminated to the clan; the realm could not bear the injustice.
translations.idiomatic: Youqian and five or six of his commanders were wiped out to the last cousin; the empire groaned at the wrong.

sentences.zh: 進，官至銀青光祿大夫、檢校左散騎常侍兼御史大夫，上柱國。

translations.literal: Jin rose to Silver Glory Light Grand Master, Investigating Censorate Left Regular Cavalry Attendant concurrent Censor Grandee, Upper Pillar of State.
translations.idiomatic: Jin climbed to Silver Glory Light Grand Master, Investigating Left Regular Cavalry Attendant and Censor Grandee, Upper Pillar of State.

sentences.zh: 史彦瓊者，為武德使，居鄴都，而魏博六州之政皆決彦瓊，自留守王正言而下，皆俛首承事之。

translations.literal: Shi Yanqiong served as Military Virtue Commissioner at Ye; the government of Weibo’s six prefectures was all decided by Yanqiong—from garrison commander Wang Zhengyan down, all bowed and served him.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Yanqiong held Ye as Military Virtue Commissioner and ruled Weibo’s six prefectures; from Wang Zhengyan the garrison commander down, everyone kowtowed to him.

sentences.zh: 是時，郭崇韜以無罪見殺於蜀，天下未知其死也，第見京師殺其諸子，因相傳曰：「崇韜殺魏王繼岌而自王於蜀矣，以故族其家。

translations.literal: At that time Guo Chongtao was killed without crime in Shu; the realm did not know he was dead, only that the capital had killed his sons; men therefore spread the word: “Chongtao killed Prince of Wei Jiji and made himself king in Shu”—for which his clan was destroyed.”
translations.idiomatic: Guo Chongtao had been murdered in Shu, but the news had not spread—only the slaughter of his sons in the capital was seen; rumor said Chongtao had killed Jiji and declared himself king in Shu, and so his house was exterminated.”

sentences.zh: 」鄴人聞之，方疑惑。

translations.literal: The people of Ye heard it and were full of doubt.
translations.idiomatic: Ye buzzed with uncertainty.

sentences.zh: 已而朱友謙又見殺。

translations.literal: Soon Zhu Youqian was also killed.
translations.idiomatic: Then Zhu Youqian was killed as well.

sentences.zh: 友謙子建徽為澶州刺史，有詔彦瓊使殺之，彦瓊秘其事，夜半馳出城。

translations.literal: Youqian’s son Jianhui was prefect of Cizhou; an edict ordered Yanqiong to kill him; Yanqiong kept the matter secret and at midnight galloped out of the city.
translations.idiomatic: Youqian’s son Jianhui governed Cizhou; orders came for Yanqiong to kill him; Yanqiong hid the command and fled the city at midnight.

sentences.zh: 鄴人見彦瓊無故夜馳出，因驚傳曰：「劉皇后怒崇韜之殺繼岌也，已弑帝而自立，急召彦瓊計事。

translations.literal: The people of Ye, seeing Yanqiong gallop out at night for no reason, panicked and spread the word: “Empress Liu, angry that Chongtao killed Jiji, has murdered the emperor and set herself up; she has urgently summoned Yanqiong to plan.”
translations.idiomatic: Seeing Yanqiong bolt at midnight without cause, Ye took fright and whispered: “The empress, enraged that Chongtao killed her son, has slain the emperor and seized the throne—she has called Yanqiong in haste to plot.”

sentences.zh: 」鄴都大恐。

translations.literal: Ye was gripped by terror.
translations.idiomatic: Terror seized the city.

sentences.zh: 贝州人有来鄴者，傳引語以歸。

translations.literal: A man from Beizhou who had come to Ye carried the tale home.
translations.idiomatic: A traveler from Beizhou heard it in Ye and carried the story back.

sentences.zh: 戍卒皇甫暉聞之，由此劫趙在禮作亂。

translations.literal: The garrison soldier Huangfu Hui heard it and thereby compelled Zhao Zaili to rebel.
translations.idiomatic: Garrison soldier Huangfu Hui heard it and forced Zhao Zaili into revolt.

sentences.zh: 在禮已至館陶，鄴都巡檢使孫鐸，見彦瓊求兵禦賊，彦瓊不肯與，曰：「賊未至，至而給兵豈晚邪？

translations.literal: Zaili had already reached Guantao; Ye’s patrol commissioner Sun Duo saw Yanqiong and begged troops to resist the rebels; Yanqiong refused, saying: “The rebels have not arrived—when they come, will it be too late to issue arms?”
translations.idiomatic: Zaili was already at Guantao; Sun Duo the patrol commissioner begged Yanqiong for troops; Yanqiong refused: “The rebels aren’t here yet—why not wait until they are?”

sentences.zh: 」已而賊至，彦瓊以兵登北門，聞賊呼聲，大恐，棄其兵而走，單騎歸於京師。

translations.literal: Soon the rebels arrived; Yanqiong took troops to the North Gate, heard the rebels’ shouts, was greatly afraid, abandoned his soldiers and fled, alone on horseback back to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: The rebels came; Yanqiong manned the North Gate, heard their battle cries, panicked, threw down his men, and rode alone to the capital.

sentences.zh: 在禮由是得入於鄴以成其叛亂者，由彦瓊啓而縱之也。

translations.literal: Zaili was thereby able to enter Ye and complete his rebellion—from Yanqiong opening the way and letting him go.
translations.idiomatic: Zaili walked into Ye and made good his revolt—because Yanqiong opened the gate and let him pass.

sentences.zh: 郭門高者，名從謙，門高其優名也。

translations.literal: Men Gao—his name was Congqian; Men Gao was his actor’s name.
translations.idiomatic: Men Gao was really named Congqian; Men Gao was his stage name.

sentences.zh: 雖以優進，而嘗有軍功，故以為從馬直指揮使。

translations.literal: Though he had risen as an actor, he had once won military merit and was therefore made commander of the Following Horse Direct.
translations.idiomatic: He had entered as an actor but once earned battle honors, so they made him commander of the Following Horse Direct.

sentences.zh: 從馬直，蓋親軍也。

translations.literal: The Following Horse Direct was essentially the imperial guard.
translations.idiomatic: The Following Horse Direct were the emperor’s own troops.

sentences.zh: 從謙以姓郭，拜崇韜為叔父，而皇弟存乂又以從謙為養子。

translations.literal: Congqian bore the surname Guo and acknowledged Chongtao as uncle; the imperial younger brother Cunyi had also taken Congqian as adopted son.
translations.idiomatic: Congqian was a Guo by birth and called Chongtao uncle; imperial brother Cunyi had adopted him as a son.

sentences.zh: 崇韜死，存乂見囚，從謙置酒軍中，憤然流涕，稱此二人之冤。

translations.literal: When Chongtao died and Cunyi was imprisoned, Congqian set wine in the army, wept in anger, and spoke of the injustice done these two men.
translations.idiomatic: When Chongtao was dead and Cunyi in chains, Congqian feasted his troops, wept, and cried out at the wrong done to both men.

sentences.zh: 是時，從馬直軍士王溫宿衛禁中，夜謀亂，事覺被誅。

translations.literal: At that time the Following Horse Direct soldier Wang Wen garrisoned the forbidden precinct; at night he plotted rebellion; the plot was discovered and he was executed.
translations.idiomatic: A guardsman named Wang Wen, posted in the palace, plotted mutiny by night; he was caught and killed.

sentences.zh: 莊宗戲從謙曰：「汝党存乂、崇韜負我，又教王溫反。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong jested with Congqian: “Your faction—Cunyi and Chongtao—wronged me, and you taught Wang Wen to rebel.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong teased Congqian: “Your friends Cunyi and Chongtao betrayed me, and you set Wang Wen on the path of treason.

sentences.zh: 復欲何為乎？

translations.literal: What do you plan to do next?”
translations.idiomatic: What are you plotting now?”

sentences.zh: 」從謙恐，退而激其軍士曰：「罄爾之貲，食肉而饮酒，無為後日計也。

translations.literal: Congqian was afraid; he withdrew and stirred his soldiers: “Empty your wealth—eat meat, drink wine, do not plan for days to come.”
translations.idiomatic: Congqian was terrified; he went back and roused his men: “Spend everything you have—feast today and leave tomorrow to chance.”

sentences.zh: 」軍士問其故，從謙因曰：「上以王溫故，俟破鄴，盡坑爾曹。

translations.literal: The soldiers asked why; Congqian said: “Because of Wang Wen, when Ye is taken the emperor will bury you all alive.”
translations.idiomatic: They asked why; Congqian said: “The emperor blames you for Wang Wen—when Ye falls he will massacre every one of you.”

sentences.zh: 」軍士信之，皆欲為亂。

translations.literal: The soldiers believed it; all wished to rebel.
translations.idiomatic: They believed him—and every man was ready to rise.

sentences.zh: 李嗣源兵反，嚮京師，莊宗東幸汴州，而嗣源先入。

translations.literal: Li Siyuan’s army rebelled and advanced on the capital; Zhuangzong went east in person to Bianzhou, yet Siyuan entered first.
translations.idiomatic: Li Siyuan’s army rose and marched on the capital; Zhuangzong hurried east to Bianzhou—but Siyuan was already inside.

sentences.zh: 莊宗至萬勝，不得進而還，軍士離散，尚有二萬餘人。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong reached Wansheng, could not advance and turned back; his soldiers scattered, yet more than twenty thousand remained.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong reached Wansheng, could not push forward, and withdrew; the army broke apart, but he still had twenty thousand men.

sentences.zh: 居數日，莊宗復東幸汜水，謀扼關以為拒。

translations.literal: After several days Zhuangzong again went east in person to Sishui, planning to seize the pass as a defense.
translations.idiomatic: Days later he went east again to Sishui, intending to hold the pass and block his enemies.

sentences.zh: 四月丁亥朔，朝羣臣於中興殿，宰相對三刻罷。

translations.literal: On the first day of the fourth month, dinghai, he held court with the ministers at Zhongxing Hall; the chancellor’s audience lasted three quarters and was dismissed.
translations.idiomatic: On the first day of the fourth month he held court at Zhongxing Hall; the chancellors were heard for three quarters of an hour, then dismissed.

sentences.zh: 從駕黄甲馬軍陣於宣仁門、步軍陣於五鳳門以俟。

translations.literal: The yellow-armor cavalry of the imperial escort formed ranks at Xuanren Gate and the infantry at Wufeng Gate to await events.
translations.idiomatic: The imperial yellow-armor horse arrayed at Xuanren Gate and the foot at Wufeng Gate, waiting.

sentences.zh: 莊宗入食内殿，從謙自營中露刃注矢，馳攻興教門，與黄甲軍相射。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong entered the inner hall to eat; Congqian from his camp bared blades and strung bows, galloped to attack Xingjiao Gate, and exchanged shots with the yellow-armor army.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong went to eat in the inner palace; Congqian rode out of camp with blades bare and bows drawn, struck Xingjiao Gate, and traded volleys with the yellow-armor guard.

sentences.zh: 莊宗聞亂，率諸王衛士擊亂兵出門。

translations.literal: Zhuangzong heard the riot and led the princes and palace guards to strike the mutineers and go out the gate.
translations.idiomatic: Hearing the uproar, Zhuangzong led the princes and guards out to fight the mutineers.

sentences.zh: 亂兵縱火焚門，緣城而入，莊宗擊殺數十百人。

translations.literal: The mutineers set fire and burned the gate, climbed the wall to enter; Zhuangzong killed several hundred.
translations.idiomatic: The mutineers fired the gate and scaled the walls; Zhuangzong cut down hundreds.

sentences.zh: 亂兵從楼上射帝，帝伤重，踣於絳霄殿廊下，自皇后、諸王左右皆奔走。

translations.literal: Mutineers shot the emperor from the tower; the emperor was gravely wounded and fell in the corridor of Jiangxiao Hall—empress, princes, and attendants all fled.
translations.idiomatic: Mutineers rained arrows from the tower; Zhuangzong was mortally wounded and collapsed in the corridor of Jiangxiao Hall—the empress, the princes, and everyone near him ran.

sentences.zh: 至午時，帝崩，五坊人善友聚樂器而焚之。

translations.literal: By the hour of noon the emperor died; Shanyou of the Five Workshops gathered musical instruments and burned them.
translations.idiomatic: By noon he was dead; Shanyou of the Five Workshops heaped instruments and set them ablaze.

sentences.zh: 嗣源入洛，得其骨，葬新安之雍陵。

translations.literal: Siyuan entered Luoyang, obtained his bones, and buried them at Yongling in Xin’an.
translations.idiomatic: Siyuan entered Luoyang, recovered his remains, and buried them at Yongling in Xin’an.

sentences.zh: 以從謙為景州刺史，已而殺之。

translations.literal: Congqian was made prefect of Jingzhou, then soon executed.
translations.idiomatic: They made Congqian prefect of Jingzhou—and soon put him to death.

sentences.zh: 《傳》曰：「君以此始，必以此終。

translations.literal: The Commentary says: “What a ruler takes as his beginning, he will surely take as his end.
translations.idiomatic: The Commentary says: “What a lord begins with, he must end with.

sentences.zh: 」莊宗好伶，而弑於門高，焚以樂器。

translations.literal: ” Zhuangzong loved actors, yet was assassinated by Men Gao and burned with musical instruments.
translations.idiomatic: ” Zhuangzong doted on actors—yet was killed by Men Gao and consumed in a fire of instruments.

sentences.zh: 可不信哉！

translations.literal: Can this fail to be believed!
translations.idiomatic: Who would not believe it!

sentences.zh: 可不戒哉！

translations.literal: Can this fail to be a warning!
translations.idiomatic: Who would not take warning!
